title: From denial to exploitation: how the Kremlin has adapted its climate disinformation
text: EUvsDisinfo – analiza: From denial to exploitation: how the Kremlin has adapted its climate disinformation. In the latest wave of climate-related narratives spread by the Kremlin, climate change is a vehicle to reinforce familiar disinformation tropes: the alleged authoritarianism and hypocrisy of the EU, Europe's supposed self-inflicted decline through sanctions against Russia, and, ultimately, the claim that Europe has no choice but to restore relations with Russia as a supplier of affordable oil and gas. Climate change used to be a fringe topic in Kremlin propaganda. It was rarely mentioned, and when it was, it was often accompanied by absurd claims or outright denial. But as the effects of climate change become increasingly difficult to ignore (including domestically in Russia), pro-Kremlin outlets have largely stopped denying its existence. Instead, they have woven it into their disinformation ecosystem, shifting from denying the problem to discrediting proposed solutions. The EU’s “green dictatorship” Russian foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) activity has become an increasingly prominent driver of energy- and climate-related disinformation. Moscow-linked proxies exploit social media to amplify misleading narratives on energy and climate policy, reinforcing anti-EU messaging and seeking to undermine public trust in European institutions and policy objectives. One of the most insidious approaches used by pro-Kremlin FIMI is to portray climate policies as covert mechanisms of control. The supposedly “ totalitarian nature ” of the EU is one of the Kremlin’s most persistent narratives, and also one of its most versatile, with new regulation adopted by the Union often being portrayed as evidence of authoritarianism. Climate and energy policies fit neatly into this framing. Measures to fight climate change and improve energy efficiency are recast as pretexts for surveillance or attacks on individual freedoms and private property: for instance, smart technologies that allow to manage electricity demand from data centres are portrayed as instruments of state control that Brussels could use to ration power for ordinary citizens. The goal here is to convince audiences that any regulatory action taken in the EU is a step towards authoritarianism, undermining their trust in democratic institutions. The ticking climate bomb Russia is sitting on a ticking climate bomb with the potential to affect the entire planet.
